title: Othniel, Ehud, and Shamgar: The First Deliverers
summary: The chapter names the nations left in Canaan to test Israel and records how Israel intermarried with them and served their gods. Then come the first three judges: Othniel, empowered by the Spirit, defeats Cushan-rishathaim; Ehud, a left-handed Benjamite, assassinates the obese Moabite king Eglon and leads Israel to victory; and Shamgar strikes down six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad.
story: Chapter 2 laid out the pattern of the book in general terms. Now the stories begin, and the pattern takes on names. Othniel's brief account is the model case, told almost entirely in the formula words of chapter 2. Ehud's story is the first full narrative, and it is vivid, violent, and darkly comic. Shamgar gets a single verse. Together they show God raising up very different people to save Israel. They also start a quiet slide: Othniel is a model judge, Ehud wins by deception, and later judges will be more compromised still. The long rest of eighty years after Ehud is the longest in the book.
historical:
The oppressors come from several directions. Cushan-rishathaim is called king of Aram-naharaim, meaning Aram of the two rivers, the region of upper Mesopotamia around the Euphrates, far to the northeast. He is not known from any other source. His name, which means something like Cushan of double wickedness, looks like an Israelite mocking nickname. Because a Mesopotamian king seems distant for a conflict with a southern judge like Othniel, some scholars suggest the original reference was to Edom, whose name looks very similar to Aram in Hebrew script, but this is a conjecture.

Moab lay east of the Dead Sea. Eglon crossed the Jordan with Ammonite and Amalekite allies and took the City of Palms, that is, Jericho or its oasis, controlling the fords and the territory of Benjamin. The Philistines, whom Shamgar fights, settled on the southern coast of Canaan in the twelfth century BC, after arriving among the groups Egyptian records call the Sea Peoples. Verse 3 names their five rulers, who governed the five main Philistine cities: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Gath, and Ekron.
cultural:
Paying tribute (verse 15) was how a subject people acknowledged an overlord: goods such as grain, livestock, silver, or cloth were carried to the king's court by a delegation. This gave Ehud access. His sword, about a cubit long (around eighteen inches or less, depending on the cubit), was hidden on his right thigh, where a guard checking a right-handed man would not look. Ehud is described in Hebrew as a man restricted in his right hand, which most take to mean left-handed, perhaps trained to use the left hand. There is irony in the fact that he came from the tribe of Benjamin, whose name means son of the right hand. Judges 20:16 mentions an elite corps of seven hundred left-handed Benjamite slingers.

The upper room was a cool chamber built on a roof, catching breezes, and it seems to have had its own toilet. The servants' assumption that the king was relieving himself (literally, covering his feet) gave Ehud time to escape. The idols near Gilgal were carved stones or images, perhaps a boundary marker. The ram's horn, the shofar, was blown to summon men to war. An oxgoad was a long wooden pole with a pointed metal tip used to drive oxen, a farmer's tool turned into a weapon.
literary: Verses 1 to 6 close the book's introduction. Othniel's story (7 to 11) is the pattern in its purest form: evil, anger, oppression, crying out, a deliverer raised up, the Spirit, victory, rest. Ehud's story (12 to 30) is a carefully told piece of narrative art, full of irony and some coarse humor at the enemy's expense. Eglon's name sounds like the Hebrew word for calf, and the fattened king is struck down like an animal for slaughter. Ehud's word from God (verse 20) is literally a thing from God, a pun on the Hebrew davar, which means both word and thing. The detailed attention to doors, keys, and the servants' embarrassment slows the pace while Ehud gets away. Shamgar's single verse (31) is a brief notice, like those of the minor judges later.

outline.t: The nations left to test Israel
The secret message and Eglon's death
Ehud rallies Israel and Moab is subdued

doctrines.note: The Spirit of the LORD came upon Othniel (verse 10), the first of several such statements in Judges. In this book the Spirit equips leaders for a particular task of deliverance, rather than describing their moral character.

God raises up deliverers through unexpected means: a left-handed man, a tribute visit, servants too embarrassed to open a door, a farmer's goad. The narrator credits the victory to the LORD (verse 28) while telling a story full of human cunning.
Each deliverance begins when Israel cries out to the LORD. The cry is not always deep repentance, but God answers it. The book shows a God who responds to the cry of the oppressed.

words.note: Za'aq, to cry out, often in distress or for help, as Israel cried out under Egyptian slavery. It marks the turning point in each cycle. It doesn't always mean repentance; it is first of all a cry of pain, and God hears it.

Ruach, spirit, wind, or breath. The Spirit of the LORD comes on Othniel and makes him able to judge and fight. In the Old Testament the Spirit often comes on particular people for particular tasks, such as leadership, craftsmanship, or prophecy.

Itter, restricted or bound. The phrase describing Ehud literally means restricted in his right hand. Most read it as left-handed. Whether this was a disability or training, the very thing that might have seemed a weakness became the means of his success.
Shaqat, to be quiet or at rest. The land had rest, forty years after Othniel and eighty after Ehud. The rest never outlasts the judge; the word marks each hard-won peace and prepares for its loss.

christ: Othniel's story is the book's model: a deliverer raised up by God, on whom the Spirit comes, who judges and saves and gives the land rest. The New Testament presents Jesus as the one on whom the Spirit rests fully (Luke 4:18, quoting Isaiah 61:1) and who gives rest to the weary (Matthew 11:28). Ehud's unlikely victory also fits a larger biblical pattern in which God uses what looks weak to overcome what looks strong, which Paul describes in 1 Corinthians 1:27. These links are thematic. Ehud's trickery and violence are not presented as a picture of Christ, who won his victory not by killing but by dying.

hard.q: How can Scripture present Ehud's deceptive assassination of Eglon as God's deliverance?
hard.a: The story is violent and involves deception, and many readers are uneasy with it. Some interpreters point out that Israel was under foreign occupation and that Ehud acted as a leader in a war of liberation, where deception of an enemy ruler was a normal part of conflict, as it is in modern wartime. Others note that the narrator says God raised up Ehud as deliverer but does not say the Spirit came on him or that God directed each act; the story reports what Ehud did without endorsing every method. Still others read the book as a whole as increasingly critical of its heroes, so that Ehud's cunning is a step toward the more troubling judges who follow. What the text clearly affirms is that God freed an oppressed people, and it leaves the reader to weigh the means.

questions: Othniel's story is short and simple. Why might the book begin with a model judge before telling the messier stories?
Ehud's left-handedness became an advantage. Where have you seen something that looked like a weakness become useful in God's hands?
Israel cried out only after eight and eighteen years of oppression. Why do people often wait so long to cry out to God?
